slides.title:
Build a research loop.
Then give it an agent.
slides.body:
A four-hour research shift at Pending, Inc.
Solar forecasting, experiment tracking, and agents that edit research code.
slides.notes: Opening, 30 seconds. This is the research team at the fictional Pending, Inc. The notebook contains real public solar observations and actual training code. We will first build the experiment, then give a fixed-model agent a limited role in changing it.

slides.title: Your team has a promising result.
slides.body:
“The new model looks better.”THE RESEARCH UPDATE · FICTIONAL SCENE

You ask which run.

Someone shares a screenshot.

You ask which code.

Someone shares a notebook called final.

There are four notebooks called final.
slides.notes: Tell the fictional scene briefly. It establishes the familiar problem of a score without the program, data, and settings that produced it. Do not imply this anecdote happened in the rehearsal.

slides.title: The Sun has supplied the data.
slides.body:
Predict what we will observe next from what we have observed so far.

First: measurements

Predict X-ray flux 30 minutes ahead.

Then: images

Predict a solar image one hour ahead.

A small teaching experiment. No operational space-weather claims.
slides.notes: Define forecasting before introducing the agent. SunPy gives astronomy-aware tools for acquiring and inspecting observations. This is not flare classification or a reproduction of a foundation-model benchmark.

slides.title: Management has another request.
slides.body: “Once the experiment works, could an agent improve it?”THE SAME FICTIONAL MANAGER
slides.notes: The joke is the escalation from doing research to automating pieces of research. The answer is a tested workflow, not a promise of better performance. Research-agent weights stay fixed; the small forecasting models are trained.

slides.title: What you will build
slides.body:
Forecast

Data, persistence, metrics.

Track

Code, settings, trained weights.

Improve

Review and test agent-written edits.

Evaluate

Freeze, compare, reproduce.

Your own notebook and project. The facilitator can read the progress you publish.
slides.notes: Show the work in order. Participants edit visible Python. Every execution is explicit. A higher score is optional; an explainable experiment is the goal.

slides.body:

The first access check is also free.

slides.title: The measurement forecast
slides.body: Predict log10 XRS-B flux. A forecast window includes observations, timestamps, and a future target.
slides.notes: GOES-15 one-minute X-ray measurements. The task is a 60-minute history predicting flux 30 minutes ahead. Explain log scaling without suggesting these models are calibrated operational forecasts.

slides.title: Dates are part of the experiment
slides.body: February 2014, UTC. Fit normalization on training data only.
slides.notes: The splits are dates, not random neighboring rows. All source observations and the target must fit inside one partition. Otherwise near-duplicate solar states can leak from training into evaluation.

slides.title: A missing observation is a gap
slides.body:
What the archive returned

GOES February 8 is absent.

Incomplete forecast windows are excluded.

What the loader must preserve

Observation time and quality flags.

The split and the reason for each exclusion.

Do not replace an absent flux measurement with zero.
slides.notes: Actual source coverage from dataset manifest. The image archive and GOES have different exclusions. Do not treat a missing measurement as evidence that solar flux reached zero.

slides.title: SunPy gives the observations context
slides.body:
```python from sunpy.map import Map observation = Map(dataset_path / "sample-aia.fits") print(observation.date) print(observation.wavelength) print(observation.unit) ```
Inspect a real FITS file. Train from the prepared, checksum-verified arrays.
slides.notes: The package is approximately 26.1 MB. Prepared arrays keep downloads small; a representative FITS file retains astronomy metadata. Acquisition code and manifest preserve source URLs, checksums, preprocessing, and exclusions. Credit NOAA, NASA/SDO, AIA, JSOC, and SunPy.

slides.title: Inspect the observations before training
slides.body:
Open 2 · Solar data.
  1. Click Load the solar dataset.
  2. Find an observation time, the image wavelength, and the dataset version.
  3. Explain why a forecast window that crosses February 10–11 must be excluded.
Done when: you can identify the inputs, target, units, and partition of a forecast.
slides.notes: Use 6 minutes. No model fit belongs in this exercise. The archive was prepared before class, so students inspect versioned data rather than waiting for thousands of downloads.

slides.title: The first model predicts no change
slides.body:
```python def persistence_forecast(split): # Latest observed value becomes the future prediction. ... ```

A difficult baseline to beat can still be a one-line function.

The baseline uses the current observation, never the future target.
slides.notes: Persistence is meaningful for correlated solar observations. A model must beat this simple prediction before complexity has demonstrated value. Do not claim persistence will win every task.

slides.title: A forecast needs a defined error
slides.body:
```python error = mean(abs(predicted_log_flux - observed_log_flux)) ```

Lower is better

The same target, transform, and units apply to every run.

The average is not the plot

Inspect the times where the forecast misses.

The observed future supplies the target. Numeric forecast quality uses a fixed metric, not an LLM judge.
slides.notes: Primary measurement metric is log-flux MAE in log10 W/m² units. Don’t average this number with image error. A trend chart and individual errors provide information the mean omits.

slides.title: Write and test persistence
slides.body:
Open 3 · Persistence.
  1. Implement persistence_forecast(split).
  2. Click Check my persistence function, then Run my persistence baseline.
  3. Inspect the observed and predicted curves. Identify one interval where copying the present misses the future.
Done when: your function returns the current observation and your saved baseline has a metric and a plot.
slides.notes: Allow 10 minutes. Local checks are free. Do not reveal the answer until students have attempted it.

slides.title: A score alone cannot reproduce a run
slides.body:
The validation error is lower.

Which source?

A loss changed yesterday.

Which data?

A gap changed the windows.

Which settings?

One run trained longer.

Each is a different experiment, even when the notebook has the same filename.
slides.notes: These are possible causes, not claims about a hidden failure in the rehearsal. Ask what information a teammate needs to rerun a result.

slides.title: These scores need their configurations
slides.body: <RunInspector />
slides.notes: Interactive illustration using two actual recorded rehearsal rows. Ask what changed before revealing the active configuration. Both runs use the same source and training budget; learning rate differs. Reproduction also requires data and executed source. No training or inference occurs in this widget.

slides.title: The learning rate changed. The budget did not.
slides.body: <RunInspector :revealed="true" />
slides.notes: Static reveal for the PDF and the live teaching sequence. The two actual runs share data, source, seed, steps and batch size. At this short budget, the lower error alone does not establish a better converged architecture.

slides.title: The program produces the forecast
slides.body: <ResearchMap :level="0" />
slides.notes: First build of the shared research diagram. Forecast model, observation and prediction stay in place throughout the progression.

slides.title: The executed code belongs to the record
slides.body: Saving a notebook and saving the code that executed are different operations.
slides.notes: Attach exact source. The model and training functions are editable. The stage receipt fingerprints source and settings.

slides.title: Keep the measurement fixed
slides.body: The model can change. The target, partition, and primary scoring rule stay fixed.
slides.notes: The primary scorer is supplied by the experiment. Learner metrics are checked against it. A revised metric creates a different question and must not retroactively improve old scores.

slides.title: Save the work needed to explain the score
slides.body: W&B runs show metrics. Artifacts preserve data, source, weights, and predictions.
slides.notes: No generic product pitch. Runs make settings and loss history comparable; artifacts preserve files for restoration and reproduction.

slides.title: Visible training, durable saving
slides.body:
```python with session.stage( "measurement/run", config=config, sources={"candidate.py": source}, inputs={"dataset": dataset_version, "split": "validation"}, ) as stage: if stage.needs_run: result = train_model(data, config) stage.record(result) ```
The notebook owns the training code. The session saves completed work.
slides.notes: Conceptual public API example. In the actual notebook run_training invokes training.train and saves weights/predictions. A completed receipt must be restored rather than repeating work on refresh.

slides.title: A restart should restore, not rerun
slides.body:
Local receipt

Which stage finished and which files it produced.

Checkpoint artifact

A versioned copy in the participant’s project.

New runtime

Restore saved results before offering the next action.

Publication retry uploads saved work. It does not launch training again.
slides.notes: Use the actual restoration behavior. An upload failure should preserve local results and clearly identify what is unpublished. Monitoring is read-only and cannot gate participant progress.

slides.title: Make the result reproducible
slides.body:
Open 4 · Track and search.
  1. Implement training_loss and my_flux_mae, then run Check my measurement code.
  2. Inspect run_training. Find where it records source, data, settings, and outputs.
  3. Open a saved run and its artifact. Identify the fields you would need after deleting the runtime.
Done when: you can match a metric to its source fingerprint and dataset version.
slides.notes: 15 minutes. Students should change the metric, then see a local wrong-value check fail and fix it. Do not make this a form-only reflection.

slides.title: Settings, architectures, and new code
slides.body:
OperationWhat changes
Hyperparameter searchValues used by an existing program
Architecture comparisonWhich implemented model runs
Agent-directed researchThe model, loss, or training program itself
We will do all three. The first two do not require a research agent.
slides.notes: This distinction is the spine of the workshop. Searching learning rates is useful, but it is not an agent inventing new code.

slides.body:

Small MLP16, 32, 16.001, .001, .00360 steps each

Seed 17. Batch size 32. The notebook records the active values.
slides.notes: These are the fixed rehearsal settings from the notebook. Short budget is deliberate for class, not a claim of tuning quality. Settings remain editable and must be recorded if changed.

slides.body:
Before ranking architectures, inspect whether training had time to learn the target scale.

In the recorded rehearsal, the short GOES models remained undertrained. Persistence won.
Keep the failed comparison. A longer uniform training budget is a new experiment.

slides.title: Run the same search and inspect a loss curve
slides.body:
Stay in 4 · Track and search.

  2. Open the Sweep and compare validation error with runtime.

slides.title: The experiments can wait ten minutes.
slides.body:
Save the checkpoint.
Leave the notebook open.
Give your own optimizer a break.

We resume at 1:40 with image predictions.
slides.notes: Ten-minute break. No new background experiments are required. Confirm checkpoint status before leaving.

slides.title: The target is now a future image
slides.body: AIA 171 Å. Prepared 64 × 64 arrays. One-hour forecasting.
slides.notes: The image task receives frames at t−60 and t and predicts t+60. The same chronological split rules apply. Larger images are an optional separate compute experiment.

slides.title: Reuse the experiment record
slides.body: The input and prediction changed shape. Source, settings, weights, and evidence still belong together. The image score uses normalized log1p intensity.
slides.notes: Do not reintroduce every product. Reuse the same record structure to make the new task less cognitively expensive.

slides.title: A forecast produces an image you can inspect
slides.body: Recorded rehearsal image forecast. The notebook shows your own prediction after training.
slides.notes: Source evidence/solar-validation.png. Use it to identify which panel is input, prediction, target, error. It is not the participant’s current result.

slides.title: Predict the full future image
slides.notes: Keep technical detail concrete. This is a tiny model for CPU class time, not a solar foundation model.

slides.title: Or predict a correction to the present
slides.body:
```python class ImagePredictor(nn.Module): def forward(self, x): correction = self.net(x) return x[:, 1:2] + correction ```

The current image supplies a starting point. The network learns the change.
slides.notes: The residual path makes persistence accessible when correction is zero. It does not guarantee better forecasting. Participants implement the branch in the actual code editor.

slides.title: Score the solar disk
slides.body:
```python error = abs(prediction - target) masked_error = error * disk_mask score = mean(masked_error.sum_per_image() / disk_mask.sum_per_image()) ```
A change outside the mask must not affect the score. Test that explicitly.
slides.notes: Pseudocode for disk-masked MAE. The real answer sums axes 1,2,3 per example before averaging. A whole-image average can hide a scientifically important small region.

slides.title: Training loss and final metric have different jobs
slides.body:
Training lossPrimary evaluation metric
Supplies gradients while fitting weightsMeasures predictions for comparison
Candidate code can change itFixed outside candidate code
The starting implementation uses squared errorThe image comparison uses masked absolute error
slides.notes: Explain why an agent might test L1 without moving the goalposts. Changing training loss is an allowed edit; changing the independent scoring metric is not.

slides.title: Compare what each model actually predicts
slides.body: Recorded validation case: convolution above, residual below. Open full comparison and evidence links ↗
slides.notes: Fresh revised-notebook rehearsal. Both rows share the same input and target timestamps. The full capture contains the native notebook score table, saved model predictions, and direct Agent Lens, run and artifact links. This is a validation example; final dates are still reserved.

slides.title: Implement and compare the image predictors
slides.body:
Open 5 · Solar images.
  1. Edit ImagePredictor.forward, training_loss, and my_image_mae.
  2. Click Check my image code. A +1 error should score 1; an off-disk change should score 0.
  3. Click Compare convolutional and residual predictors. Inspect both forecasts.
Done when: you can identify the selected manual model and show a case where its forecast is wrong.
slides.notes: 20 minutes. Learners need an attempt before worked answers. Same data and training budgets apply to both models. Results are selected using validation only.

slides.title: Now the agent can edit the program
slides.body: Management has automated the proposal. You still review the diff.
slides.notes: Introduce the meta layer only after students have built a working experiment. The agent gets evidence and a constrained edit request. It can be mistaken.

slides.body:
Research agentForecasting model
JobPropose code editsPredict solar observations
WeightsFixed throughoutTrained on training dates

No post-training of the research agent occurs in this workshop.
slides.notes: Explicitly correct possible carryover from the Harness² agent workshop. There all runtime model weights stayed fixed. Here small forecasting models train normally.

Find read_validation_evidence.

Then inspect the proposal.

slides.title: Choose what the research agent may inspect
slides.body:
Open 6 · Research agent.
  1. Inspect select_validation_evidence(record). Keep active settings and validation results, then click Check my evidence selection.
  2. Check that reserved-date predictions and scores are excluded.
  3. Read the mission. Name one proposed test that could show an edit did not help.

slides.notes: 12 minutes. Code selection is the lesson, not copying an event identifier by hand. Use small visible checks for allowed split and supported source.

slides.title: Two candidates start from the same parent
slides.body: Harness²-inspired: our probes train forecasting weights and include validation scores.
slides.notes: Introduce competing hypotheses. This is a teaching adaptation of Harness² Propose–Probe–Compose (https://github.com/google-research/harness2/tree/1cfe254e8d25b15f37048c3730134686abe60335). Upstream task refinement uses execution evidence without ground-truth feedback. Here the agent explicitly receives validation metrics and edits an ML training program. A larger network is not automatically better.

slides.title: Review the actual change, then test it
slides.body: Fresh rehearsal proposal: .square() became .abs(). Review is not evidence of a gain. Full capture ↗
slides.notes: Actual round-one proposal in the revised browser rehearsal. This frame is cropped to the source diff and explicit review control. The full capture includes the agent-attributed rationale. We have not inferred a performance benefit from that rationale. Only the subsequent probe can measure it.

slides.title: Each proposed program must run
slides.body: Use the same training and validation data. Keep failed runs visible.
slides.notes: Show exact source fingerprints and receipts. If an attempt fails to train, preserve its failure; don’t coerce a missing score to zero.

slides.title: Composition reviews the probes
slides.body: KEEP retains the source. Its next probe is a new execution, not a new executable version.
slides.notes: Dashed lines mean reviewed evidence. They do not mean both candidates were adopted. This was a major ambiguity in older branch drawings.

slides.title: A composition is another proposal until tested
slides.body: The proposed file must match the source the probe executes.
slides.notes: A combined version can introduce new behavior. Even if both component candidates passed, the composition needs an execution. Retaining the parent preserves the source fingerprint.

slides.title: The next round uses the previous result
slides.body: Carry the adopted source and an evidence-backed lesson into round two.
slides.notes: Both rounds remain on the solar image task. The selection policy uses validation error. Repeated editing is not proof of recursive performance gains.

slides.title: Run round one, one decision at a time
slides.body:
Inspect next_research_action in 6 · Research agent.
  1. Propose two code changes. Read both diffs.
  2. Confirm review of Candidate A → Test Candidate A. Confirm review of Candidate B → Test Candidate B.
  3. Record my comparison, then Request a composition.
Done when: you can point to each candidate’s files, training result, and Agent Lens conversation.
slides.notes: Work alongside learners. Review actions are free; testing is explicit. Keep this slide visible during the first half of round one.

slides.title: Test the composition, then repeat
slides.body:
Continue the same workbench.
  1. Confirm review of composition, then Test the composition.
  2. Click Save the adopted version and lesson. Check whether the parent was retained.
  3. Repeat the process in round two using the previous outcome.
Done when: both rounds have a tested selection and rejected alternatives remain inspectable.
slides.notes: 15 minutes. A valid KEEP outcome completes the exercise. If calls are slow, inspect saved evidence and label replay rather than pretending an edit ran.

slides.title: Every branch should explain a decision
slides.body: <ResearchBranches :level="5" :interactive="true" />
slides.notes: Optional two-minute interactive recap. Keyboard-accessible nodes explain the process. This diagram is an illustration; the notebook branch view opens actual records.

slides.title: The search ends before final evaluation
slides.body:
Persistence

Copy the latest observed image.

Manual selection

Best implemented model on validation.

Agent selection

The last valid adopted code and weights.

Freeze source and weights. No more selection using the reserved dates.
slides.notes: The final image comparison has three versions on the same later windows. The measurement comparison is separate. The final stage loads weights rather than fitting again.

slides.title: Final inference loads the saved weights
slides.body:
```python model = build_model(input_shape, frozen_config) model.load_state_dict(saved_weights) model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): prediction = model(final_inputs) ```
There is no optimizer step in this stage.
slides.notes: Illustrative inference excerpt. Validate the actual execution uses the frozen model rather than silently retraining. The fixed scorer sees future targets; the candidate program does not during improvement.

slides.title: Compare the same forecast windows
slides.body:
Case identityPersistenceManualAgent-selected
Same input timestampsPrediction + errorPrediction + errorPrediction + error
Same target timestampTrace or receiptExecuted sourceExecuted source
Weave and EvalTables use stable case IDs to align predictions across versions.
slides.notes: Native EvalTables has returned HTTP500 in the recorded rehearsal. Show the notebook and Weave comparison when unavailable. Never label a fallback W&B Table as native EvalTables.

slides.title: Evaluate the frozen versions
slides.body:
Open 7 · Final evaluation.
  1. Click Freeze versions and evaluate reserved dates.
  2. Select one shared case. Inspect its prediction, observed future, and error for every version.
  3. Open its training record, source, and Agent Lens evidence. Keep image and measurement scores separate.
Done when: all versions are represented, including missing results and failed publication.
slides.notes: 20 minutes. Score differences are evidence from these dates and this run. Do not count pixels or neighboring timestamps as independent studies.

slides.title: Quality, effort, and execution are separate
slides.body:
QuestionEvidence
Did forecasts improve?Matched final predictions and fixed metrics
What did improvement cost?All proposals, probes, retries, and compute
Did execution get more reliable?Errors, missing outputs, and recovery traces
slides.notes: A smoother execution may not produce a better forecast. A tiny score change may not justify a large search. Inference and notebook compute billing are separate.

slides.title: Your teammate should be able to reopen the result
slides.body:
Run

Settings, metric, loss history.

Artifact

Source, data, weights, predictions.

Trace

Agent requests, edits, tests, decisions.

The Report explains what changed and links to those records.
slides.notes: Explain the evidence chain in ordinary language. Do not make facilitator monitoring a substitute for storing scientific outputs.

slides.title: Publish the result you can defend
slides.body:
Use your own comparison.
  1. State one code change and the result it produced on reserved dates.
  2. Include an example where the forecast failed or changed little.
  3. Click Publish my conclusion. Reopen one result from its saved artifact.
Done when: another person can trace your claim to its code, run, prediction, and score.
slides.notes: Eight minutes. Permit a negative finding. If publication fails, save the conclusion and use publication-only retry.

slides.title: The agent can propose the next experiment.
slides.body:
You now have the part that makes the proposal testable.

Keep the data version. Save the executed source. Inspect the prediction. Measure on dates the search did not use.

Management may still ask for a better number. You can now explain the one you have.

slides.title: The image scorer ignores off-disk pixels
slides.body:
```python def my_image_mae(prediction, target, disk_mask): errors = np.abs(prediction - target) * disk_mask per_image = errors.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) per_image /= disk_mask.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) return float(per_image.mean()) ```

Test zero error, constant +1 error, and an error only outside the mask.
slides.notes: Code validated against small deterministic fixtures. Production scorer remains independent.
